column2: follow-up question (asked when this keyPoint is uncertain; must not contain the answer)
When a town is hit by floods, why does fixing the problem need many groups working together rather than one authority giving orders?
A municipal body installs street lights. Which part of that story is the institution and which is the process of planning, maintaining and taking feedback?
What did colonial rule leave behind in governance, and what made India's situation different from many other former colonies?
Where do India's national and Supreme Court mottos come from, and what idea of a ruler's duty lies behind them?
Name the seven features of good governance and the groups who must each play a part for it to work.
What can stop a government scheme from reaching everyone it is meant for?
How can a citizen in a far-off village get a government service without travelling to an office, and why does that matter in a huge country?
What must a person have before an online government service can help them, and what must the government therefore ensure?
What questions does a government answer when it makes a policy, and how does it learn whether the policy is working?
Is a school's rule on mobile phones a public policy? What features would make a policy truly public?
List, in order, the main steps from noticing a public problem to improving a policy after it is in use.
Which features of the education policy's making show consultation and expert advice, and when was it approved?
If a government wants everyone to have good healthcare, which part of that is the aim, which the plan and which the concrete service people receive?
Name some concrete schemes that carry out a national health policy, and what the 'policy' level adds above them.
Who raises an issue like a water shortage in the Assembly, who requests a zebra crossing, and who actually carries out a scheme in a district?
What can an NGO, a company and an international health body each add to a public programme?
In a national sports policy, what does each level of government and the private sector contribute, and why does it all have to be coordinated?
What can an ordinary student or citizen do to help public institutions work better?
